Para1:
"Large language model inference on a single GPU is increasingly governed less by raw floating point throughput and more by the movement of tensors through memory. In autoregressive decoding, each newly generated token requires the model to attend to all previously generated tokens, and the intermediate key and value tensors for those tokens must be retained across steps. This creates a persistent key value cache, often called the KV cache, whose size grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. On a single accelerator, the cache competes with model weights, activations, and temporary buffers for a finite amount of high bandwidth memory. As a result, the practical speed of decoding is often limited by how quickly the GPU can read the cache and the weights, rather than by how many matrix multiply accumulate operations it can perform. Speculative decoding and flash attention are two techniques that address different parts of this problem. Speculative decoding changes the algorithmic structure of generation so that multiple candidate tokens can be verified in one forward pass, while flash attention changes the implementation of attention so that the same computation can be performed with far less memory traffic. Understanding how they interact is essential for building efficient single GPU inference systems."

"The KV cache is the central data structure in transformer inference. For each layer, the attention mechanism computes queries, keys, and values from the hidden state. During prefill, the model processes the entire prompt in parallel, producing a large block of keys and values. During decoding, each new query token must be multiplied against all previous keys to produce attention scores, and the resulting weights are used to combine the corresponding values.
